The total power change simulated in the distribution network is fed to a generator model, which models the frequency of the synchronous grid. When power demand exceeds the scheduled total generation, the frequency will decline, and the opposite will happen if demand is less than total generation. These dynamics are modeled in Simulink, with a block representing a synchronous generator which follows the differential equation 𝑑𝜔 𝜔2 (𝑃 −𝑃 ) 0 𝐺 𝐿 = 𝑑𝑡 2𝐻𝜔 𝑃 𝐵 In which P is the base rated power of the generator, P is the current generation, P is the current load, ω is the B G L 0 nominal frequency of the system in radians per second, and H is the system inertial constant in seconds. The choice of H allows us to model the system under various conditions. A choice of H close to 4 seconds models, a grid primarily composed of synchronous generation, while lowering this number allows modeling of the system assuming less inertia, with a higher share of inverter-based resources. The frequency modeled in Simulink by the generator block described above is sampled by a control block every two seconds (0.5 Hz). The frequency error (the gap between the nominal and measured frequency) is given to a proportional-integral controller which generates a control signal for the DERs to adjust output. In order to properly model this full system in a way that accurately mimics the traditional control methods used by utilities to dispatch such grid services, we use a similar OpenADR connection to deliver these control signals to the devices. 22 The power setpoint generated by the controller in Simulink is sent over UDP to another process on the same machine which runs an OpenADR VTN. The VTN takes each new power setpoint and sends an OpenADR event to a VEN which controls the devices as described in task 8.1. In this way, the HIL system can properly simulate a power system and send commands to real hardware in real-time. Figure 5: HIL Simulation Results The figure above shows how the HIL system reacts to a pulsating disturbance load of 50 kW on a simulated power system of 5 MW total load. When the load ramps up, the frequency quickly drops, as it takes two seconds for the controller to sample the frequency, generate a new setpoint, and communicate it to the devices. However, once the control signal is produced, the system is able to arrest the frequency decline and begin to return the frequency back to nominal. These preliminary results show that the system can perform simulation and control in real time.
